23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)

25	- **In scope:**

27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.

109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).

112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.

120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.

10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractPurposeThe inborn errors of immunity (IEIs) are a group of heterogeneous disorders. Although autoimmunity frequently coexists with IEIs, the manifestations vary greatly across different disorders. Most cases are recognized only after clinical symptoms emerge, impacting outcomes. However, limited research has been reported on how to achieve early identification. In this study, we aim to identify early or subclinical autoimmune reactivity and associated immunological patterns in patients with IEIs, and to explore differences among various IEI genotypes.MethodsThe clinical records and laboratory data of 26 patients were reviewed. Immunophenotypes were evaluated by multiparametric flow cytometry. Genetic findings were confirmed by whole-exome sequencing (WES). Autoantibodies were detected via antigen microarray analysis.ResultsWe focused on several types of inborn errors of immunity that are prone to autoimmune diseases including 5 CD40LG mutations, 4 RAG1/2 mutations, 1 IL2RG mutation, 1 DOCK8 mutation, 1 SH2D1A mutation, 1 FAS mutation, 1 FOXP3 mutation, 1 TNFAIP3 mutation, 6 STAT3 gain-of-function (GOF) mutations, 3 STAT3 loss-of-function (LOF) mutations, and 2 CTLA4 mutations. Approximately 31% had clinical autoimmune manifestations, while several asymptomatic patients showed elevated autoantibodies. Some patients exhibited broad IgG and/or IgM autoantibody profiles targeting nuclear, cell membrane, and organ-specific antigens, which were associated with certain clinical features or immune subsets, such as increased double-negative T (DNT) cells and marginal zone B (MZB) cells.ConclusionAntigen microarrays may enable early identification of autoimmune risk in IEI patients even before symptoms arise. Patients with genotypes such as STAT3 GOF were more likely to develop autoimmunity. The breadth of IgM autoantibodies correlated positively with MZB cell frequency, and higher DNT cell levels were significantly associated with clinical autoimmunity, suggesting potential utility for early risk stratification.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10875-026-02024-y.Keywords: Inborn errors of immunity, Antigen microarray, Autoimmunity, Marginal zone B cells, Double-negative T cells

14	## Introduction
15	
16	Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs) are closely associated with autoimmunity [1–5]. Studies have shown that a considerable proportion of IEI patients, approximately 20% develop autoimmune diseases during the course of their illness [6]. In some patients, autoimmune diseases, such as autoimmune cytopenias, enteropathies, endocrine disorders, or rheumatologic diseases, may be the initial or primary manifestations of IEIs, without obvious signs of infection. Notably, the presence of autoimmunity in IEI often indicates a more severe disease course and is associated with a poorer prognosis compared to those with only infectious susceptibility [7, 8]. These clinical observations underscore the intricate and multidimensional relationship between autoimmunity and immunodeficiency [1, 9, 10].
17	
18	However, in current clinical practice, autoantibody testing is usually performed only after autoimmune disease becomes clinically evident, limiting opportunities for early detection and intervention. Early identification of autoantibodies before symptom onset could enable timely management, potentially preventing irreversible damage and improving outcomes.
19	
20	Autoimmune manifestations in IEIs are highly heterogeneous across distinct genetic defects, implying diverse pathogenic mechanisms [11]. For example, CTLA-4 deficiency frequently causes severe, multisystem autoimmunity, with central nervous system involvement in nearly one-third of cases, such as autoimmune encephalitis, optic neuritis, or other inflammatory neurologic syndromes [7, 12]. By contrast, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is characterized by a predisposition to autoimmune cytopenia and rheumatologic autoimmune disease [13, 14]. These patterns suggest that different genetic defects elicit divergent pathways of autoimmunity, warranting studies of genotype-specific mechanisms and tailored management.
21	
22	Antigen microarrays have recently emerged as high-throughput platforms for autoantibody profiling, simultaneously detecting broad antibody panels from minimal sample with superior throughput, sensitivity, and antigen coverage compared with conventional evaluation of autoantibodies such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunofluorescence [15, 16]. This technology enables efficient delineation of autoantibody signatures and may facilitate early identification of latent autoimmunity in IEI, supporting earlier preventive or therapeutic interventions.
23	
24	In light of these considerations, we profiled autoantibodies in 26 patients with IEIs using an antigen microarray.We aimed to identify early or subclinical autoimmune reactivity, explore associated immunological patterns across different genetic subtypes, assess concordance with conventional assays, and evaluate the potential utility of this high-throughput platform as an exploratory early warning tool for autoimmune risk in IEIs. Subclinical autoimmunity in this context is defined as the presence of a broad and significantly elevated repertoire of autoantibodies, particularly high-affinity IgG autoantibodies targeting specific organs or nuclear antigens—in the absence of overt clinical autoimmune disease, which distinguishes it from the physiological, low-affinity natural autoantibody repertoire that is typically IgM-dominant. We compared autoantibody spectra across genetic subtypes, assessed concordance with conventional assays, and evaluated the exploratory utility of this high-throughput platform as an early warning tool for autoimmune risk in IEIs.
25	
26	## Methods
27	
28	This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Children’s Hospital of Fudan University (No. 2022 − 179). All guardians of patients provided written informed consent for enrollment in this study.
29	
30	### Patients and Clinical Data
31	
32	Patients diagnosed with IEIs on the basis of the presence of clinical manifestations, functional test findings and related gene mutations confirmed by whole-exome sequencing were included in our study. We summarized the clinical data of the patients. The parents of each patient provided written informed consent. Blood samples from healthy controls were collected at the National Children’s Medical Center under approved ethical protocols.
33	
34	### Genetic Analysis
35	
36	Genomic DNA was isolated from whole blood using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was conducted with the IDT xGen Exome Research Panel v2 Kit (Integrated DNA Technologies, Coralville, IA).
37	
38	### Immunoglobulin Assays
39	
40	IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were detected by nephelometry; UniCAP (Pharmacia, Uppsala, Sweden) was used to assess IgE levels.
41	
42	### Conventional Flow Cytometric Analysis
43	
44	Whole blood was stained with monoclonal antibodies as previously reported [17], after which red blood cells were lysed using Pharm Lyse™ (BD Biosciences). The stained cells were then analyzed on a FACSCalibur flow cytometer (BD, USA), and data were processed using FlowJo software.
45	
46	### Multiparametric Flow Cytometry
47	
48	High-throughput flow cytometry analysis was conducted. In brief, 51 surface antibodies were organized into six panels. Peripheral whole blood was collected in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) anticoagulant tubes. Whole-blood samples were incubated with the antibody panels, lysed using Lysing Solution (BD, USA), and subsequently washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Data acquisition was performed on a CytoFLEX LX Flow Cytometer (Beckman Coulter, USA) using CytExpert v2.4 software (Beckman Coulter, USA). After exclusion of debris and doublets, live CD45⁺ lymphocytes were gated by FSC/SSC. T-cell subsets included total T cells (CD3⁺), CD4 T cells (CD3⁺CD4⁺), CD8 T cells (CD3⁺CD8⁺), double-negative T cells/DNT (CD3⁺CD4⁻CD8⁻), TCRαβ⁺ DNT (CD3⁺CD4⁻CD8⁻TCRαβ⁺), and γδ T cells (CD3⁺TCRγδ⁺). T-cell maturation on CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ gates was defined by CD27/CD45RA as naïve (CD27⁺CD45RA⁺), central memory (CD27⁺CD45RA⁻), effector memory (CD27⁻CD45RA⁻), and terminal effector (CD27⁻CD45RA⁺). B-cell compartments were identified as total B cells (CD19⁺), naïve (CD19⁺CD27⁻IgD⁺), marginal zone–like (CD19⁺CD27⁺IgD⁺), class-switched memory (CD19⁺CD27⁺), transitional (CD19⁺CD24^highCD38^high), and plasmablasts (CD19⁺CD38^high, often CD27^high). Results were reported as percentages of CD45⁺ lymphocytes or of the immediate parent population, as indicated.
49	
50	### Conventional Evaluation of Autoantibodies
51	
52	Autoantibodies were detected using the Kangrun Bio autoantibody detection kit (Guangzhou Kangrun Biotech Co., Ltd., China) following the manufacturer’s instructions. For the ELISA method, serum samples were incubated with antigen-coated wells for a specified time, followed by the addition of enzyme-conjugated secondary antibody and substrate solution. The colorimetric signal was then measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader. In parallel, the Indirect Immunofluorescence Assay (IFA) involved incubating serum samples with slides containing HEp-2 cells, followed by incubation with a fluorescently labeled secondary antibody. The samples were examined under a fluorescence microscope, and specific fluorescence patterns indicated the presence of autoantibodies. Both methods included positive and negative controls to ensure the reliability and accuracy of the results.
53	
54	### Antigen Microarray Analysis
55	
56	Plasma samples from 26 patients were analyzed using an antigen microarray (GeneCopoeia, USA). The array included 120 IgG- and IgM-specific autoantigens. The experimental procedure was as follows: serum samples were first heat-inactivated and pretreated with DNase I. Samples were then diluted 1:100 in PBS and applied to the microarray slide for hybridization with the immobilized antigens. The binding of IgG and IgM antibodies was detected using Cy3-labeled anti-human IgG secondary antibody (1:1000) and Cy5-labeled anti-human IgM secondary antibody (1:1000), respectively. Slides were scanned with a Lux-Scan 10 K-A scanner (CapitalBio Corporation, China) at laser wavelengths of 532 nm (IgG) and 635 nm (IgM). The resulting images were converted to raw data using LuxScan_v3.0 software (CapitalBio Corporation, China). For each antigen, the normalized fluorescence intensity (NFI) was calculated by subtracting the local background and negative control (PBS) signals. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calculated as follows: SNR = (median foreground − median background)/standard deviation of the background. Finally, positive controls at various dilutions were used, and the NFI values were normalized using a robust linear model. A threshold of a ≥ 3-fold increase in NFI compared to the mean NFI of healthy controls was selected to define significantly elevated autoantibody levels. This threshold was chosen to stringently filter out background noise and physiological variations, thereby highlighting pathologically relevant autoantibody responses.
57	
58	### Statistical analysis
59	
60	The measurement data are presented as the means, medians, ranges, and interquartile ranges (IQRs). Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). Heatmaps were drawn with Heatmapper (www.heatmapper.ca) [18].

62	## Results
63	
64	### Patient Characteristics
65	
66	In this study, we identified 26 Chinese patients with IEIs (15 males and 11 females). The clinical features of the 26 patients are shown in Table 1. The genotypes of patients according to IEI category are shown in Fig. 1, including 5 CD40LG mutations, 4 RAG1/2 mutations, 1 IL2RG mutation, 1 DOCK8 mutation, 1 SH2D1A mutation, 1 FAS mutation, 1 FOXP3 mutation, 1 TNFAIP3 mutation, 6 STAT3 gain-of-function (GOF) mutations, 3 STAT3 loss-of-function (LOF) mutations, and 2 CTLA4 mutations. The median age of onset of IEI was 11.5 months (range, 0 months to 63 months). The median age at genetic diagnosis was 20 months (range, 3 months to 153 months), and the diagnostic delay was 10.5 months. In this cohort of 26 patients, the majority were male, and a spectrum of pathogenic mutations was identified across ten distinct immunodeficiency-related genes. CD40LG mutations, which are consistent with X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome (XHIGM), were observed in 5 patients (P1–P5). STAT3 GOF mutations were detected in 6 patients (P6–P11), whereas STAT3 LOF mutations were detected in 3 patients (P12–P14), reflecting the phenotypic diversity associated with STAT3 dysregulation. RAG1 or RAG2 mutations, which are associated with defects in V(D)J recombination, were detected in 4 patients (P15–P18); mutations in IL2RG (P19), CTLA4 (P20–P21), TNFAIP3 (P22), SH2D1A (P23), FAS (P24), DOCK8 (P25), and FOXP3 (P26) were each detected in a single patient, highlighting the genetic heterogeneity of the cohort. The patients in our cohort presented with a broad spectrum of clinical symptoms. Respiratory tract infections were the most common cause of hospital admission. A total of 9 patients initially presented with upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), and the median age of these patients was 15.7 months (range, 2 months to 48 months). Seventeen (65.3%) patients reported recurrent respiratory infections. In 3 patients (P5, P8 and P12), fever was noted as an initial symptom. Several patients developed severe lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs), such as pneumonia and lung abscess. In addition, otitis and pharyngolaryngitis were reported in a subset of patients, indicating involvement of the ear, pharyngeal, and laryngeal regions. Fifteen patients (57.7%) had significant gastrointestinal symptoms, and 3 patients (P3, P4 and P5) had peptic ulcers. Lymphoproliferative manifestations (lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly) occurred in 11 patients (42.3%). Other presentations included cutaneous and mucous membrane manifestations (such as eczema and alopecia in 8/26, 30.8%), growth retardation (3/26, 11.5%), nervous system disorders (5/26, 19.2%), and congenital heart defects (3/26, 11.5%). Among our patients, 8 (30.8%) were considered to be affected by autoimmunity. In 3 patients, autoimmunity involved the hematologic system and manifested as hemolytic anemia. A diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) was considered in one patient. One patient received a diagnosis of Behçet’s disease, and another was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Two patients were diagnosed with hypothyroidism, one of whom was also considered to have arthritis.

103	### Autoantibody Analysis
104	
105	We tested 35 serum samples from 26 patients and 9 healthy individuals. Specific information can be found in Table S1. More than 120 proteins representing autoantigen epitopes were immobilized on the autoantigen microarray to assess IgM and IgG antibody reactivity in patient serum samples. The NFI values of the IgG and IgM autoantibodies are shown in Figs. 2 and 3. In this study, all 26 enrolled patients presented elevated levels of autoantibodies to varying degrees compared with healthy individuals. Although the overall autoantibody profiles of the patients were broad, certain autoantibodies were frequently detected at significantly higher levels among those with IEIs (Fig. 4a-b). Anti-α-actinin IgG was the most common IgG autoantibody, with all 26 patients showing 3-fold higher NFIs. Elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) IgG was observed in 80.7% (21/26) of the patients, and a 3-fold higher NFI was observed in 61.5% of the patients (16/26), whereas the 3-fold higher NFIs for anti-thyroglobulin (Tg) IgG and anti-myelin basic protein (MBP) IgG were both 42.3% (11/26). In addition, 53.8% of patients (14/26) demonstrated a 3-fold increase in the NFI of anti-lipopolysaccharide (LPS) IgG. Other frequently detected IgG autoantibodies included anti-EBNA1, anti-SSA/Ro52, anti-nucleosome Ribo P2 protein, and anti-centromere protein centromere protein A (CENP-A), all of which were elevated to varying extents in subsets of patients. Notably, although 10 patients did not present with clinical manifestations of autoimmune disease, their levels of IgG autoantibodies were still significantly elevated compared with those of healthy individuals.

113	With respect to IgM autoantibodies, almost all patients responded to multiple autoantigens, with the levels of numerous IgM autoantibodies—such as anti-histone H1, MBP, ssRNA, myosin heavy and light chain, and heparan sulfate—being significantly elevated in the majority of patients. 114	
115	In this study, one of the five patients with CD40LG mutations was clinically diagnosed with IBD and presented significantly elevated autoantibody levels. We found that the NFIs of 85 IgG autoantibodies and 115 IgM autoantibodies in this patient was greater than those observed in healthy individuals. Notably, 7 IgG autoantibodies had 3-fold higher NFI levels; these autoantibodies primarily targeted nuclear antigens, thyroid-specific proteins, and nervous system-related proteins. Another patient diagnosed with Behçet’s disease had only mildly elevated autoantibody levels, with elevations observed in only 10 IgG autoantibodies. Additionally, three patients demonstrated significantly elevated IgM autoantibody levels, with more than 110 elevated IgM autoantibodies. Among the six patients with STAT3 GOF mutations, one patient (P6) was clinically diagnosed with hypothyroidism and had notably elevated autoantibody levels. We found that the NFIs of 48 IgG and 114 IgM autoantibodies in this patient exceeded those in healthy individuals, with 3-fold higher NFIs in IgG autoantibodies against thyroid-specific proteins (TPO and Tg). Compared with healthy individuals, another patient (P8) diagnosed with hypothyroidism and arthritis had only mildly elevated autoantibody levels, with increased NFIs observed for 25 IgG and 70 IgM autoantibodies. Interestingly, compared with healthy individuals, one patient (P11) without clinical autoimmune manifestations displayed significantly elevated autoantibody levels, with higher NFI values for 72 IgG and 81 IgM autoantibodies, including 13 IgG autoantibodies with 3-fold higher NFIs; these autoantibodies were predominantly directed against nuclear antigens, cytoplasmic/membrane proteins, and cytokines. Among the three patients with STAT3 LOF mutations, none exhibited clinical autoimmune symptoms. However, two patients (P13 and P14) displayed significantly elevated autoantibody levels. Compared with the healthy individuals, patient P13 presented elevated NFI for 112 IgG and 79 IgM autoantibodies, including 36 IgG autoantibodies with 3-fold higher NFIs against nuclear antigens, thyroid-specific proteins, circulating proteins, and nervous system-related proteins. Patient P14 had increased NFIs for 77 IgG and 57 IgM autoantibodies. Among four patients with RAG1/2 mutations, one patient clinically diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) had mildly elevated IgG autoantibody levels but significantly elevated IgM autoantibody levels, with 3-fold higher NFIs in nearly all tested IgM autoantibodies. Compared with healthy individuals, another patient with a RAG2 mutation had elevated NFIs for 123 IgM autoantibodies. Compared with healthy individuals, one patient with an IL2RG mutation lacked clinical autoimmune symptoms but presented significantly elevated autoantibody levels, with elevated NFI values for 111 IgG and 118 IgM autoantibodies. One patient with a CTLA4 mutation who was clinically diagnosed with AIHA had only mildly elevated autoantibody levels. Compared with healthy individuals, one patient with a TNFAIP3 mutation who was clinically diagnosed with type I diabetes had significantly elevated autoantibody levels, with increased NFI values for 67 IgG and 104 IgM autoantibodies. A patient with a hemizygous SH2D1A mutation presented clinically with autoimmune hepatitis-like symptoms, yet conventional autoantibody tests were negative. This study revealed significantly elevated autoantibody levels, with increased NFI values for 98 IgG and 117 IgM autoantibodies compared to those of healthy individuals, including 10 IgG autoantibodies with 3-fold higher NFI levels primarily targeting nuclear antigens, cytoplasmic/membrane proteins, and circulating proteins. One patient with a DOCK8 mutation lacked typical autoimmune symptoms clinically but had significantly elevated autoantibody levels compared with healthy individuals, with elevated NFI values for 97 IgG and 35 IgM autoantibodies. These autoantibodies included 51 IgG autoantibodies with 3-fold higher NFIs that predominantly targeted nuclear antigens, cytoplasmic/membrane proteins, circulating proteins, and organ-specific proteins. 117	### Comparison Between Routine Evaluation of Autoantibodies and Antigen Microarray Analysis
118	
119	The results of the routine evaluation of autoantibodies from these patients with IEIs are listed in Table S2. Among the 26 patients included in this study, nine (P4, P11, P13, P14, P15, P19, P22, P23, and P24) had significantly elevated autoantibody levels according to antigen microarray analysis. In these patients, more than half of the tested autoantibodies exhibited NFI values that were markedly higher than those of healthy individuals, despite negative results in routine clinical autoantibody assays. Additionally, five patients presented with clinical manifestations of autoimmunity. For these individuals, both routine evaluation of autoantibodies and antigen microarray analysis revealed significantly increased levels of relevant autoantibodies. For example, patient P6 was clinically diagnosed with hypothyroidism; routine evaluation of autoantibodies was positive for SSA and revealed a markedly elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb) level (> 1064 IU/ml). The results of the microarray analysis further confirmed substantial increases in the levels of thyroid-associated antibodies, including TPO and Tg antibodies. Patient P8 presented with hypothyroidism and arthritis; routine evaluation of autoantibodies revealed ANA, MPO-ANCA, RNP/Sm, SSB, Scl-70, and histone antibodies. The microarray results corroborated these findings, demonstrating significant elevations in the levels of thyroid-related antibodies (TPO and Tg) as well as histone and fibronectin antibodies. Notably, two additional patients presented with clinical symptoms of autoimmunity despite negative results for the routine evaluation of autoantibodies, yet the antigen microarray revealed a broad spectrum of significantly elevated autoantibodies. Patient P4 was diagnosed with IBD, and routine evaluation of autoantibodies was negative; however, the results of the microarray revealed marked increases in the levels of autoantibodies against alpha-actinin, TPO, Ro/SSA (52 kDa), LPS, Tg, CENP-A, and MBP. In patient P22, who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, routine evaluation of autoantibodies was also negative, but the results of a microarray revealed significant increases in the levels of several autoantibodies, including those against alpha-actinin, troponin-I, islet antigen 2 (IA2), interferon-alpha1 (IFN-A1), interferon-beta (IFN-B), LPS, La/SSB, and angiotensin II receptor (AGTR). Furthermore, seven patients (P11, P13, P14, P15, P19, P23, and P24) neither exhibited overt clinical symptoms of autoimmunity nor tested positive on routine evaluation of autoantibodies. Nevertheless, antigen microarray analysis revealed that these individuals also had significantly elevated levels of autoantibodies.

133	## Discussion
134	
135	Our cohort of 26 patients with inborn errors of immunity (IEIs) encompassed a broad spectrum of genetic defects known to predispose to immune dysregulation and autoimmunity. Approximately 31% of the patients met the criteria for clinical autoimmunity, but some patients lacked a clear diagnostic basis, which hindered the diagnosis and effective intervention of autoimmunity. Different types of IEIs may present with distinct autoimmune manifestations in clinical practice. The present cross-sectional analysis primarily identifies patterns of early or subclinical autoimmune reactivity and associated immune correlates.
136	
137	In the CD40LG-deficient group, all patients had profound hypogammaglobulinemia with low IgG/IgA requiring IVIG. Antigen microarray nevertheless detected multiple autoantibodies, predominantly IgM, consistent with previously described mechanistic models of defective T-cell (Treg) development, increased IgM autoantibodies, and impaired peripheral B‑cell tolerance in CD40L deficiency [21]. One patient had Behçet’s disease; another had IBD with markedly increased DNT and γδ T cells, yielding an autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (ALPS)‑like phenotype which suggests the potential involvement of DNT expansion in autoimmune enteropathy [22, 23]. Conventional autoantibody screens can be negative despite broad microarray reactivity. These findings indicate that T-B-cell interaction defects resulting from CD40L deficiency not only lead to hypogammaglobulinemia but also may disrupt peripheral immune tolerance mechanisms and promote the generation of aberrant autoantibodies.
138	
139	Patients with GOF mutations in the STAT3 gene presented in infancy with immune dysregulation. Two patients had overt autoimmunity with elevated autoantibodies; the remainder showed subclinical broadening of autoantibody profiles on microarray. This aligns with the known early and multisystem autoimmunity in STAT3 GOF [24–26], mechanistically linked to effector T‑cell hyperactivation with relative Treg deficiency [24, 27]. Conversely, None of the three patients with LOF mutations in the STAT3 gene had typical autoimmune disease, aligning with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) phenotypes [28]. These findings suggest pediatric STAT3 LOF may harbor subclinical autoantibodies, potentially driven by chronic, occult infection‑related immune dysregulation.
140	
141	Among the four patients with RAG1 or RAG2 gene mutations, one patient had AIHA, high IgM, and expanded DNT cells—an ALPS‑like immunophenotype with multiple autoantibodies [22, 23]. RAG deficiency frequently features anti‑cytokine autoantibodies, such as anti-IFN-α and anti-IFN-ω, especially in CID‑G/AI, consistent with our cohort [29, 30]. Another patient showed elevated autoantibodies without overt autoimmunity; in CID‑G/AI, immature B cells preferentially generate polyreactive autoantibodies, promoting their expansion [29, 31].Despite the expected rarity of autoimmunity in X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID) caused by an IL2RG gene mutation, this patient had markedly elevated autoantibodies. The striking increase in IgM indicates intrinsic aberrant autoantibody generation, potentially related to maternal microchimerism or expansion of residual immune clones [32, 33].One patient harboring a heterozygous mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene clinically presented with diabetes mellitus but without recurrent infections. Microarray detected multiple islet‑ and inflammation‑related autoantibodies, supporting immune‑mediated diabetes and a broader inflammation‑associated autoimmunity profile [34–36].One patient with a FAS gene mutation exhibited increased DNT cells with reduced memory B cells and plasmablasts. Across subgroups, higher DNT percentages paralleled elevated autoantibody levels, suggesting that Fas-mediated peripheral tolerance defects underpin both heightened autoantibodies and clinical autoimmunity [29].
142	
143	In this study, a subset of patients who tested negative for autoantibodies by conventional assays were unexpectedly found to have numerous positive autoantibody signals when assessed by antigen microarray. Specifically, nine patients lacked detectable autoantibodies on routine clinical screening and exhibited no overt autoimmune symptoms; nevertheless, antigen microarray analysis revealed abnormally elevated NFI values at more than half of the antigen sites tested. These findings suggest that conventional testing may fail to identify latent autoimmune predispositions due to restricted antigen repertoires and limited sensitivity for low-titer antibodies. Therefore, antigen microarrays may serve as a valuable complement to standard autoantibody assays in clinical practice, providing a more comprehensive assessment of underlying autoimmune risk in patients with IEIs.
144	
145	The mechanisms underlying the development of autoimmune diseases in patients with IEIs are highly complex and involve disruption of immune tolerance, dysregulation of immune regulatory functions, and defects in immune apoptosis [1, 37]. In this study, we identified a positive correlation between the proportion of MZB cells and the levels of IgM autoantibodies in patients with IEIs. As innate-like B cells, MZB cells can rapidly produce natural IgM antibodies upon antigenic stimulation [38].These antibodies are often polyreactive and include low-affinity IgM that recognizes self-antigens. Therefore, patients with an increased proportion of MZB cells may be more prone to generate IgM autoantibodies. Notably, this correlation was not observed for IgG autoantibodies. Furthermore, we observed an increased proportion of DNT cells in patients with IEIs and autoimmune manifestations. Previous studies have demonstrated that DNT cells can secrete large amounts of proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-17, thereby participating in the regulation of autoimmune responses [39]. These results are associative and hypothesis-generating, suggesting that MZB and DNT cells may play important roles in the autoimmune mechanisms underlying IEIs.
146	
147	The identification of broad autoantibody profiles in patients without clinically overt autoimmune disease underscores the concept of subclinical autoimmunity. These findings carry substantial clinical implications, as early detection may guide intensified monitoring protocols and enable timely interventions to prevent irreversible organ damage. Although the present study is cross-sectional in design, longitudinal follow-up of the cohort is planned to evaluate the predictive utility of these subclinical autoantibody signatures for the subsequent development of overt autoimmune disease.
148	
149	Despite these strengths, our study has several limitations. The genetic and clinical heterogeneity of the cohort mirrors real-world practice in IEI and constitutes an important asset of the analysis. Nevertheless, genotype-specific interpretations (such as STAT3 LOF, IL2RG, and DOCK8 variants) are based on limited patient numbers and should therefore be viewed as exploratory. Where possible, future investigations involving larger cohorts would benefit from alternative analytical strategies, such as stratifying IEIs according to shared pathogenic mechanisms (such as immune dysregulation versus combined immunodeficiency), to further refine the interpretation of autoantibody profiles.
150	
151	## Conclusion
152	
153	In this retrospective cohort of 26 patients with IEIs, autoimmune reactivity emerged early and heterogeneously across genotypes. While 31% met criteria for clinical autoimmunity, antigen microarrays uncovered broad autoreactivity in many individuals who were negative by conventional tests, indicating underdetection by routine panels. STAT3 GOF conferred the highest autoimmune risk, whereas STAT3 LOF showed subclinical profiles; RAG and CD40LG defects exhibited ALPS-like or IgM-skewed autoreactivity. IgM autoantibody breadth correlated positively with MZB cells frequency, and elevated DNT cells associated with clinical autoimmunity. Integrating genetics, multiparametric flow cytometry, and antigen microarrays suggests potential utility for earlier risk stratification and mechanism-guided monitoring in IEIs.

119	The results of the routine evaluation of autoantibodies from these patients with IEIs are listed in Table S2. Among the 26 patients included in this study, nine (P4, P11, P13, P14, P15, P19, P22, P23, and P24) had significantly elevated autoantibody levels according to antigen microarray analysis. In these patients, more than half of the tested autoantibodies exhibited NFI values that were markedly higher than those of healthy individuals, despite negative results in routine clinical autoantibody assays. Additionally, five patients presented with clinical manifestations of autoimmunity. For these individuals, both routine evaluation of autoantibodies and antigen microarray analysis revealed significantly increased levels of relevant autoantibodies. For example, patient P6 was clinically diagnosed with hypothyroidism; routine evaluation of autoantibodies was positive for SSA and revealed a markedly elevated thyroid peroxidase antibody (TPOAb) level (> 1064 IU/ml). The results of the microarray analysis further confirmed substantial increases in the levels of thyroid-associated antibodies, including TPO and Tg antibodies. Patient P8 presented with hypothyroidism and arthritis; routine evaluation of autoantibodies revealed ANA, MPO-ANCA, RNP/Sm, SSB, Scl-70, and histone antibodies. The microarray results corroborated these findings, demonstrating significant elevations in the levels of thyroid-related antibodies (TPO and Tg) as well as histone and fibronectin antibodies. Notably, two additional patients presented with clinical symptoms of autoimmunity despite negative results for the routine evaluation of autoantibodies, yet the antigen microarray revealed a broad spectrum of significantly elevated autoantibodies. Patient P4 was diagnosed with IBD, and routine evaluation of autoantibodies was negative; however, the results of the microarray revealed marked increases in the levels of autoantibodies against alpha-actinin, TPO, Ro/SSA (52 kDa), LPS, Tg, CENP-A, and MBP. In patient P22, who was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, routine evaluation of autoantibodies was also negative, but the results of a microarray revealed significant increases in the levels of several autoantibodies, including those against alpha-actinin, troponin-I, islet antigen 2 (IA2), interferon-alpha1 (IFN-A1), interferon-beta (IFN-B), LPS, La/SSB, and angiotensin II receptor (AGTR). Furthermore, seven patients (P11, P13, P14, P15, P19, P23, and P24) neither exhibited overt clinical symptoms of autoimmunity nor tested positive on routine evaluation of autoantibodies. Nevertheless, antigen microarray analysis revealed that these individuals also had significantly elevated levels of autoantibodies.
